newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia hopes for more foreign funds - agency.
newsitem.headline: Croatia hopes for more foreign funds - agency.

text.p: Croatia is hoping to attract more foreign funds from private and institutional lenders to finance post-war reconstruction and kickstart the economy, but has set a $250 million annual ceiling, national agency HINA reported.

It said Finance Minister Bozo Prka conducted talks in Washington this week with World Bank and German and U.S. bank officials on their involvement in a number of projects to spur Croatia's economic recovery.
Prka also met representatives of credit rating agencies which are assessing its borrowing potential before a planned issue of Eurobonds, aimed at attracting big private investors.

They have been increasingly drawn to Croatia with its stable economy and fresh investment opportunities since the Dayton peace agreements in December last year put an end to four years of bloodshed in former Yugoslavia.
So far, the cash-strapped country has depended on loans from the World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF), which have together pledged over $400 million in aid.

The bank recently approved another $100 million to restore regional infrastructure. This may be expanded to cover Eastern Slavonia, an are now held by separatist Serbs which is due to be integrated with the help of international community.

Repairs of war damage, estimated at almost $30 billion, may have to be stretched over a number of years Croatia stuggles to provide for a whole range of pressing costs from care of war victims to company restructuring and opening of new jobs.

Analysts say this may be a good chance to close down some technologically outdated industrial facitilities, that had piled up losses since well before 1991 and are not likely to catch pace with more profitable competition at home or abroad.
The IMF, which is considering further support for Croatian reforms, said during a recent mission that overall borrowing must be kept within reasonable budget limits.

To do that, the government would have to tighten the reign on current expenditures so as to meet public needs while not widening the budget gap above three percent of the economy. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
